title: Talking to yourself by name
hookLine: third-person self-talk helped people stay calmer under stress

cards: "Okay, Maria. You've done harder things than this. Slow down." A woman is saying it to the mirror in an office bathroom, five minutes before a job interview, half embarrassed in case someone walks in.

Talking to yourself, out loud, in the second person, as if you were somebody else. It looks like a strange habit. Psychologists have tested it, and the small change it makes, from I to your own name, is today's lesson.

teach.h: A SPEECH WITH NO TIME TO PREPARE.
teach.b: First, the experiment. Ethan Kross and colleagues, writing in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, gave people a stressful task: a speech, with very little time to prepare.

Beforehand, some thought through their feelings using I; others used their own name and you. The name-users reported less shame afterward, and observers rated their speeches as better. Second, why it might work.
The researchers call it distanced self-talk.

teach.h: DISTANCE: ADVICE AS IF TO A FRIEND.
teach.b: Your name puts a little space between you and the moment, the space you have when a friend calls with a problem. It's often easier to see clearly into a friend's trouble than your own, and your name borrows some of that.

In Psalm 42 the singer speaks to his own soul as if it were someone else in the room. In the King James Bible: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?" He doesn't scold himself.
He asks, and then he answers with hope. Talking to oneself is old, and it can be gentle. Fourth, the fine print.
This is lab research with a speech in a room, not a cure for every hard day; distance helps with the moment, but it doesn't replace help when things are heavy. And the voice matters.
Calling yourself by name in a harsh boss's voice is just the inner critic with better grammar.
The research and the psalm both point to the coach, not the critic.

how: Some people use distanced self-talk before stressful moments, quietly addressing themselves by name or as "you" to steady themselves, much as the Psalms speak to the soul.

games.q: what does “talking to yourself by name” mean?
o: a sign of stress that therapists try to stop
coaching yourself with your own name, as you would a friend
repeating your name to boost how confident you look

games.q: talking to yourself by name: tap the pairs.
p: your name and you, not I
why art thou cast down, O my soul?

s: in the study, people who used their own name reported less shame after the speech
the name-users also had their speeches rated as better by observers.
talking to yourself by name is a new trick invented in a lab
the lab tested it, but the psalm already has a singer speaking to his own soul.
any voice works, as long as you use your name
a harsh voice with your name in it is still the critic. the research and the psalm both point to the coach.

games.q: you have five minutes before a tough meeting. which sentence matches what the study tested?
o: "you've got this. slow down." said with your own name first.
games.why: people who used their own name and you felt less shame and spoke better. distance gives you a friend's view of your own moment.

practice: Bring to mind one thing ahead of you that feels hard: a conversation, a deadline, an appointment you've been dreading.
Silently, speak to yourself the way a good coach would, using your own name: you've prepared for this, take it one piece at a time.
Notice how it sounds addressed to you rather than coming from you; some people of faith bring the same hard thing into prayer.

wordCard.voice: Talking to yourself by name. Distanced self-talk: your own name and you, the way you'd speak to a friend. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: by name. Said kindly, the way you'd talk to a friend. Until tomorrow.
